Question 1

Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=⟨e2y+4x,x7−y2⟩ through the boundary of the square −1≤x≤0,−1≤y≤0.

a
4
b
5
c
2
d
−5
e
−4
Submit

decision.explanation: By Green's theorem in flux form, the outward flux is the integral of the divergence. Here ∇·F = 4−2y, so the flux is ∫_{−1}^0∫_{−1}^0(4−2y) dx dy = [4y−y²]_{−1}^0 = 5.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{2y}+4x,\,{x}^{7}-{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 0,-1\le y\le 0.$
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071160/assets/09acd3df62b333bdaeb7553599507d4dbad7412ef2770b00e8fc8855b38a774e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{2y}+4x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}-{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 0}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,dy \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

a

decision.explanation: Green's theorem gives outward flux as the integral of the divergence, which is 3+1=4. The region is 0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤x^5, so the flux is ∫₀¹∫₀^{x^5}4 dy dx = 4∫₀¹x^5 dx = 2/3.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,{x}^{7}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{5}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071160/assets/00bceda1bdf4f515646b3a1e8476f1eadde721aa52dbc9be9c7e866bcab99d3b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{5}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\,dx \\  & =4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,{x}^{7}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{5}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071160/assets/00bceda1bdf4f515646b3a1e8476f1eadde721aa52dbc9be9c7e866bcab99d3b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{5}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\,dx \\  & =4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
